name: todo
title: A todo list on the command line
pitch: Add, list and finish tasks from your terminal, saved in a file. It's small, and it walks you through what makes Rust different: structs, enums with match, and errors you have to handle.

steps.do: Create the project with `cargo new todo` and run it.
steps.hint: If cargo isn't installed, rustup.rs explains how to get it.
steps.why: cargo creates the project, builds it and runs it. Every Rust project you'll meet uses it.

steps.do: Write a Task struct (its text, and whether it's done) and print one.
steps.hint: `#[derive(Debug)]` above the struct lets you print it with `{:?}`.
steps.why: Rust asks you to describe your data before using it. derive asks the compiler to write some common code for you.

steps.do: Keep tasks in a Vec<Task>, add a few and list them with their numbers.
steps.done: the list prints with numbers, starting at 1.
steps.hint: `.iter().enumerate()` gives each item with its index.
steps.why: Vec is Rust's growable list. Iterators like enumerate are how Rust loops over things without index mistakes.

steps.do: Read the command from the arguments: `cargo run -- add "buy bread"`, `cargo run -- list`.
steps.hint: `std::env::args()` gives the words; `.collect::<Vec<String>>()` makes a list of them. The `--` separates cargo's arguments from yours.
steps.why: Everything after `--` goes to your program, not to cargo: a convention many tools share.

steps.do: Turn the command into an enum and handle it with match.
steps.done: an unknown command prints how to use the program.
steps.hint: `enum Command { Add(String), List, Done(usize) }`, and a function that turns the arguments into one.
steps.why: An enum lists every possible case, and match makes you handle each of them: forget one and the program doesn't compile. That's one of Rust's best features.

steps.do: Save the tasks to a JSON file with serde, and load them at start.
steps.done: the tasks are still there at the next run.
steps.hint: Add serde (with the derive feature) and serde_json to Cargo.toml; `#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)]` on Task.
steps.why: Crates are Rust's libraries, and Cargo.toml lists the ones your project uses. serde turns your structs into JSON and back with one line of derive.

steps.do: Replace every unwrap() with Result and ?: a missing file, broken JSON, a task number that doesn't exist.
steps.done: each mistake prints a clear message instead of a panic.
steps.hint: Make functions return `Result<…, String>` (or Box<dyn Error>), use `?` to pass errors up, and print them once in main.
steps.why: unwrap() says "this can't fail". When it can, Rust makes you decide what happens. `?` keeps that decision short to write.

steps.do: Mark a task as done, and delete a task.
steps.hint: `get_mut(i)` gives a task you can change, `remove(i)` deletes one. Remember the user counts from 1.
steps.why: Borrowing a value to change it (&mut) is the core of Rust's rules: one writer at a time, checked by the compiler.

steps.do: Optional: due dates, or arguments parsed with the clap crate.
steps.hint: clap's derive API turns a struct into a full command-line parser.
steps.why: Good crates save days of work. Learning to read their documentation on docs.rs is part of learning Rust.
